Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: High-frequency event study (a form of “narrow-window” difference-in-differences).  
• Why appropriate?  
  – The exact timing of FOMC announcements is known to the minute; equity returns measured over a tight window around the announcement are virtually free of contamination by other news.  
  – Policy surprises are observed from federal-funds-futures price changes within the same window, giving a quasi-experimental shock that can be treated as exogenous.  
  – Because the surprise is continuous, we estimate dose–response: larger (absolute) surprises should move equity prices more.  

To decompose channels, we embed the surprise measure in a Campbell-Shiller VAR; the surprise serves as an instrument for the one-step change in the short rate, allowing us to trace out how the shock maps into revisions of expected dividends, real rates, and excess returns. Hence the strategy is:  
Step 1 – Event-study regression: equity return on monetary-policy surprise.  
Step 2 – VAR-based decomposition, treating the same surprise as an external instrument (IV) for the unexpected one-period change in the short rate.  

================================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: mps_t ≡ “monetary-policy surprise” = (actual change in target – expected change inferred from fed-funds-futures) / (days in contract month) expressed in basis points. It is continuous and can be positive (tightening surprise) or negative (easing surprise).  

Control condition (counterfactual): return on the same security in the absence of a surprise, approximated by:  
  a) The equity return during the same intra-day window on (i) FOMC days with zero surprise and (ii) all non-FOMC days, or  
  b) The return in the 30-minute window ending 30 minutes before the announcement (pre-trend test).  

Treatment timing / event date:  
• Pre-1994: use the first NY-Fed open-market-operation (11:30 a.m.) the day after a decision (standard in the literature).  
• Feb 1994–Dec 2002: use the time-stamped FOMC press release (usually 14:15 EST).  
The outcome window is [t0, t0 + 60 minutes].  

================================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 (No simultaneous confounders) – Within a 60-minute window no other systematic news moves equity prices in a way correlated with the policy surprise. Plausible because macro data releases are scheduled earlier in the morning; we will remove events that coincide with payroll, CPI, etc.  

A2 (No anticipation) – The unexpected component extracted from futures contracts fully captures market expectations; surprises are orthogonal to pre-announcement returns. Reasonable given liquidity of futures market, but we can test it by regressing pre-window returns on surprises (should be zero).  

A3 (Local linearity / stable mapping) – The impact of a surprise on asset prices is linear (or log-linear) within the narrow window; no feedback within the event window. Plausible over one hour.  

A4 (Exogeneity as instrument) – When used as an IV inside the VAR the surprise affects the state vector only through the policy rate. This is the Kuttner (2001) logic; plausibility strengthened by the very narrow window.  

================================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
T1 Macro releases on the same morning (employment report, CPI).  
 Fix: Drop those dates or include MMS surprise measures as controls in the regression.  

T2 Inter-meeting moves often coincide with crisis-time information (e.g., LTCM, 9/11).  
 Fix: Include a crisis dummy; run robustness excluding inter-meeting actions.  

T3 Measurement error in futures-implied expectations (thin trading pre-1994).  
 Fix: (i) Instrument the measured surprise with changes in the 1-month-ahead futures rate within the same window; (ii) run subsample post-1994 when contracts are liquid; (iii) weight events by futures volume.  

================================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)
library(sandwich)

# ---- 1. Load data ----
# Assume three csv files: events.csv, returns.csv, mms_surprises.csv
events <- fread("events.csv")       # date, time, target_change_bp, mps_bp
returns <- fread("intraday_ret.csv") # date, window_ret (in %)
mms <- fread("mms_surprises.csv")   # date, payroll_surprise, cpi_surprise, ...

# ---- 2. Merge & construct variables ----
setDT(events); setDT(returns); setDT(mms)

dat <- merge(returns, events, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
dat <- merge(dat, mms, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)

# FOMC indicator
dat[, fomc_day := !is.na(mps_bp)]

# Control windows: pre-window return (-60 to 0 minutes)
# assume pre_window_ret already in returns.csv
# Generate demeaned surprise
dat[, mps_std := scale(mps_bp, scale = FALSE)]

# ---- 3. Main event-study specification ----
# Outcome: window_ret
# Standard errors: heteroskedasticity-robust (HC2)
reg_main <- feols(window_ret ~ mps_bp + payroll_surprise + cpi_surprise | 0,
                  data = dat[fomc_day == TRUE], vcov = "hetero")
summary(reg_main)

# ---- 4. Placebo (pre-window) check ----
reg_placebo <- feols(pre_window_ret ~ mps_bp, 
                     data = dat[fomc_day == TRUE], vcov = "hetero")
summary(reg_placebo)

# ---- 5. Subsample robustness: post-1994 only ----
reg_94 <- feols(window_ret ~ mps_bp + payroll_surprise + cpi_surprise | 0,
                data = dat[fomc_day == TRUE & date >= "1994-02-04"], vcov = "hetero")

etable(reg_main, reg_placebo, reg_94)

# ---- 6. VAR decomposition (sketch) ----
# Requires monthly data ‘var_monthly.csv’ with six variables including
# eq_return, div_growth, real_rate, etc. and the policy surprise series.
library(vars)
var_dat <- fread("var_monthly.csv")
var6  <- VAR(var_dat[, -c("date")], p = 12, type = "const")
# Structural identification via external instrument
library(ivreg)
# (details omitted for brevity)
```

================================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
Theory (discounted cash-flow) predicts that a 25-bp unexpected tightening should lower broad equity prices roughly 1 % to 1.5 % (Campbell, 1991; Gurkaynak, 2005).  
Channel priors:  
• Real-rate channel dominates in the very short run (higher discount rate).  
• Dividend-growth revisions slightly negative (tightening lowers demand).  
• Risk-premium channel ambiguous but likely contributes ~25 % of total move.  

================================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (event-study / external-instrument design)  
C1 Precise timing of treatment: 1  
C2 No anticipation / parallel trend in pre-window: 1  
C3 No concurrent confounders in window: 0.5 (some overlap with data releases)  
C4 Exogeneity of instrument in VAR: 0.5 (reasonable but not airtight)  
C5 Stable outcome measurement, no spillovers: 1  

Overall = 4 / 5.
